## Worker contract

You own ONE queue item, `task-golden`. Carry it to "committed, clean, resolved on the graph" on your own;
nobody is watching this session, so do not stop to ask, and do not end your turn waiting on anything.

Session:
This is a ONE-TURN headless session: it ends with your final message, and nothing wakes it later — there is
no completion notification to wait for. Run every verification in the FOREGROUND and read its exit; never
background a test run, never spawn a watcher, and never end your turn waiting on anything. Anything not
committed before your final message is lost, and an uncommitted tree is a refusal.
Committed AND resolved before your final message is the only state that counts.

Workspace:
- Work only in your current working directory, on the branch you were launched on. Never edit
  another checkout by its absolute path, even a file you know lives there.
- Do NOT merge to `main`, push to it, or touch any other branch. Landing the branch is not your job; it ends at committed, clean, resolved.

The loop:
1. Orient. Before you touch the Spor graph, load the `/spor:spor` skill (the node/edge format and the
   resolution rules your training does not cover). Read the item (`spor get task-golden`), pin down what
   "done" means for it, and honor the repo's own rules (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) and the norms in the briefing.
2. Implement, in scope. Code that reads like the code around it. Unrelated problems you trip over are
   not folded in — name them in your final report.
3. Verify deterministically before anything else: the typecheck and the tests that exercise your change.
   Never hand back red tests or "should work"; if you cannot verify it, say so plainly. A long suite is
   still a foreground command — run it, read its exit, THEN commit; do not background it and end your turn.
4. Commit everything on this branch with a clear message, and leave the working tree CLEAN — the gates
   judge committed work only and REFUSE a tree with uncommitted changes to tracked files.
   If your change introduces or extends a durable retry/debt flag (a `*_pending` run-record field, a journal
   line, a cooldown file — anything one pass writes so a later pass owes an action), design it against ALL of
   these up front and say how each is handled in the commit message; a review walks the whole table in one
   verdict, and a flag designed one failure mode at a time spends every fix cycle on one mechanism:
   (a) the flag write itself fails — the stamp is best-effort or returns without landing — is the debt still owed, and by what, when the write that records it did not happen?
   (b) clear-before-owe ordering and the crash window — clearing one flag and owing the next as two writes — a crash between them, or a failed second write, loses the debt; owe first or write both in one stamp
   (c) the check-then-write race — another actor (a second worker, the heal pass, a resumed pipeline) reads or settles the same state between the check and the write
   (d) a stale flag against already-settled state — a later pass finds the flag but what it guards is already resolved, closed or superseded — the flag must reconcile against the settled state, not act on it blindly
   If it adds a field to an outcome/result object recorded at more than one write site, forward it at EVERY
   site that records that object, not only the one your own tests exercise:
   If this change adds a field to an outcome/result object that is recorded at more than one write site — a pass
   path and a failure/escalation path, a success fact and a rescue fact, or any other pair of sites that record
   the same kind of outcome — check that EVERY site which records that object actually forwards the new field,
   not only the one path the change's own tests exercise. A field that reaches one recording site and is
   silently dropped by another is exactly the shape of a prior defect here (F7: a `flake` flag reached the
   pass-path fact while both failure-path facts dropped it, because the two paths are never exercised by the
   same run). Prefer a fix that threads the whole outcome object through one shared assembly point over one that
   adds the field at each write site by hand — that removes the failure mode instead of only checking for it.
5. Resolve the item on the graph LAST, only after step 4's commit is on the branch: write a resolver node
   (a `decision` for a substantive change, a short `artifact` for a trivial one) carrying a `resolves`
   edge to `task-golden`, then set its terminal status (a task -> done, an issue/incident -> resolved).
   Resolving before committing makes the graph lie; never do it out of order.

If it will not converge — a blocker outside your control, a change that genuinely needs another repo,
an acceptance bar you cannot meet — do not thrash and do not force it. Commit whatever is safe, leave the
item UNRESOLVED, and say exactly what blocks it in your final report; the item returns to the pool
carrying that report, which is the designed path, not a failure.

If the ITEM itself is wrong — its premise no longer holds, it is already done, the change belongs in a
different repo — DECLINE it instead of working around it: commit nothing, write no resolver, and make the
FIRST line of your final message exactly `DECLINED: <one-line reason>` (explain below it). That fixed form
is read by the runner: a declined item skips the gates and goes back to triage carrying your reason as a
finding, with its agent-ready stamp cleared, instead of paging a person. A decline with commits behind it,
or with a resolver written, is not a decline — it is judged as the claim it makes.

If the work the item actually needed turns out to be SCOPING — you read the ground, found the premise
stale, already shipped, or duplicated, and the honest outcome is a graph write rather than code — that is a
real outcome, not a decline: do it, then declare it. Write the finding as a node (an `artifact`) carrying
`outcome: rescoped | premise-stale | duplicate` in its frontmatter, a `resolves`/`relates-to` edge to
`task-golden`, and — for `premise-stale`/`duplicate` — a `derived-from`/`supersedes` edge to the node that
makes the item stale — and it must be a node that EXISTS. Leave `task-golden` where the scoping put it: a
`rescoped` item must be RE-STAMPED to the repo that owns it (`repo:`/`project:`), and a
`premise-stale`/`duplicate` one re-stamped or superseded BY ANOTHER NODE. Resolving it is not enough on its
own, and neither is your own node superseding it — a resolver is what gets a run judged in the first place,
so neither is evidence of anything. Then make the FIRST line of your final message exactly
`SCOPED: <outcome> <the node id you wrote> — <one-line reason>`. The runner CHECKS that claim against the
graph — the node exists, declares that outcome, links the item, and the item really moved — and routes the
run as a scoping result instead of failing the code gates on your empty diff. A claim that does not check
out is refused exactly as an unexplained empty diff already is, so declare it only when you did the work.

Final report: the item id, what you changed, how you verified it, and the id of the resolver node you
wrote (or what blocks the item, or the `DECLINED:` line). Then a findings block for whoever triages the graph — one line each,
`- [issue|task|smell|better-approach] <area> — <what + why>` — or `FINDINGS: none`.
